title: Inheritance and Autopsy
premise: Wren Coldharbour, coroner of the fading town of Marrow's Bend, autopsies a drowned woman wearing clothes stolen from his own closet—and finds a note in her pocket addressed to him in handwriting he buried three years ago. The note belongs to Ada Voss, the witness who vanished after testifying against the Coldharbour family trust, a woman everyone, including Wren, insists is dead. As Wren follows her trail through the town's falsified death records and its rotting dynastic wealth, he discovers the 'witness' is alive, hidden by the very people sworn to protect her, and that his own memory of her death was surgically edited into him. In the end, Wren must choose between preserving the lie that keeps Marrow's Bend solvent and exposing the truth that will cost him his name, his office, and possibly his life—choosing love against duty at last.
about_author: Tamsin Voss spent a decade as a rural records clerk before turning to fiction, a job she credits for teaching her how small towns keep their dead organized and their living complicit. She writes mysteries from a farmhouse full of filing cabinets, where every character is filed under a name they may not deserve.

chapters.title: The Weight of Water
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A drowned woman washes up below the old mill dam, dressed in clothes from Wren's own closet—his late mother's coat, his father's scarf. He performs the autopsy alone, hands steady, mind not. Emotional beat: dread disguised as professionalism; the first crack in his ordered world.

chapters.title: Alphabetical Dead
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Filing the Jane Doe, he cross-references missing persons and finds no match—but the woman's dental work matches records sealed by court order, signed off by Judge Ellery Crane, an old family friend. Beat: unease deepens as Wren realizes the record itself is lying to him.

chapters.title: A Note in Her Pocket
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Sewn into the victim's lining: a scrap reading 'Ask Wren about the winter of the flood,' in handwriting identical to letters Wren burned three years ago—letters from Ada Voss, the witness declared dead. Beat: vertigo; grief and suspicion entangle.

chapters.title: Everyone Swears She Drowned
chapters.summary: Wren interviews townsfolk—Pastor Hale, shopkeeper Ida Brum, Deputy Sorrel—who all recount, word for word identically, the story of Ada's drowning. Their sameness terrifies him more than any lie would. Beat: isolation; the town closes like a fist.

chapters.title: The Trust That Owns the Town
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, with flashbacks. He digs into the Coldharbour Family Trust, which holds the mill, the clinic, the cemetery deeds—and learns his own salary flows through it. Beat: complicity; he has been paid to look away all along.

chapters.title: What the Flood Took
chapters.summary: Dual timeline via Wren's recovered journal pages. Three years ago, Ada testified that the trust's dam failure killed four workers and was covered up; days later she 'drowned.' Wren remembers attending her funeral but cannot recall her face. Beat: memory as unreliable architecture.

chapters.title: The Second Body
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Deputy Sorrel is found hanged in the evidence locker, ruled suicide within hours—before Wren can examine him. Someone above Wren now controls the paperwork. Beat: fear becomes personal; the machinery turns on its own.

chapters.title: Ida Brum's Locked Room
chapters.summary: Wren POV. Ida, the only interviewee who hesitated, lets him into her back room: forty years of trust ledgers, and a photograph of Ada alive last spring. Ida begs him to stop before he's 'corrected' too. Beat: an ally found, and endangered.

chapters.title: Corrected
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Searching county archives, he finds his own medical file: a three-day hospitalization after Ada's death, 'treatment for grief' administered by Dr. Pell of the trust clinic. His memories were treated, not healed. Beat: horror of self-betrayal; he cannot trust his own past.

chapters.title: Dr. Pell's Gentle Hands
chapters.summary: Wren confronts Pell, who speaks in soothing euphemisms about 'memory hygiene' and warns that Ada's survival is a kindness Wren shouldn't undo. Pell offers him a choice: another treatment, or silence. Beat: temptation of comfortable lies.

chapters.title: The House That Remembers
chapters.summary: Wren returns to his childhood home on trust land and finds a hidden room behind his mother's wardrobe—Ada's hiding place once, stocked with her notes mapping the trust's crimes. Beat: love rekindled through evidence; the past made physical.

chapters.title: Winter of the Flood
chapters.summary: Ada's recovered notes, read in her voice. She documents the dam sabotage, the payoffs, and her escape plan—and names the one person she trusted with her life: Wren. Beat: heartbreak; he was meant to be her way out and became her burial instead.

chapters.title: Judge Crane's Mercy
chapters.summary: Wren POV. Crane admits signing the false death certificate—not for malice, he claims, but because Ada begged to disappear and the town couldn't survive the trial. 'Mercy is just corruption with good manners.' Beat: moral ambiguity sharpened.

chapters.title: They Know You Know
chapters.summary: Wren's home is searched, Ida's back room burns overnight, and a trust lawyer delivers a severance offer with a one-way train ticket enclosed. Beat: pressure peaks; the cost of continuing is named aloud.

chapters.title: The Grave With No Name
chapters.summary: Wren exhumes the plot sold as Ada's grave and finds it empty except for her testimony tapes—she faked her death and hid the evidence where only a coroner would look. Beat: hope resurrected; the dead woman planned for him all along.

chapters.title: Listening to the Dead
chapters.summary: Wren plays the tapes through the night: workers' families, bribed officials, Pell's clinical logs. He understands the drowned woman wore his clothes deliberately—a message only he could decode. Beat: resolve hardening into purpose.

chapters.title: The Woman Below the Mill
chapters.summary: Following the tapes' final clue, Wren finds Ada alive at the flooded mill's lower level, hiding with the last witness—the drowned woman's sister, who died getting the message out. Reunion laced with guilt: she watched him forget her. Beat: love against duty, face to face.

chapters.title: Pell Comes Calling
chapters.summary: Pell and trust enforcers corner them at the mill. Ada bargains with evidence of Pell's unauthorized treatments; Wren stalls with procedural authority as coroner. A violent escape leaves the mill burning. Beat: climax ignites; allies bleed.

chapters.title: In Session
chapters.summary: Climax. At an emergency town meeting, Wren presents the tapes, ledgers, and his own treatment file, forcing Crane to recuse and the trust's charter to collapse under state scrutiny. Pell flees; the town must hear what it paid to ignore. Beat: truth as public wound.

chapters.title: What We Bury, What We Keep
chapters.summary: Aftermath. Wren resigns as coroner rather than sign another softened report; Ada chooses to stay and rebuild rather than vanish again. They bury the drowned sister properly, by name. Beat: grief honored; duty redefined as honesty.

chapters.title: New Records
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, months later. The trust dissolves, the dam is condemned, and Wren takes over the town archive, rewriting the falsified files entry by entry. Ada works beside him. Beat: quiet repair; memory tended like a grave.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Wren's POV. Walking the cemetery at dusk, he names each resident aloud—including those the town tried to erase—and plants Ada's flowers on the empty plot that saved them both. Beat: peace earned; invisibility chosen freely at last.
